lessons.title: Daily Bite
lessons.objective: One card a day to stay sharp.

payload.prompt: What is the pit cycle?

options.text: The rhythm of green-flag stops, when teams pit in a similar window.
One lap when every car is required to pit.
The fastest pit stop of the day.

explanation.correct: Right. As fuel and tires run down, teams pit in a similar window and the running order reshuffles. Reading the cycle is how fans see who gained or lost.
explanation.incorrect: No lap is mandatory for everyone, and the cycle is not about one fast stop. It is the rhythm of green-flag stops that reshuffles the order.

payload.prompt: Steep banking, as at Bristol and Talladega, lets cars carry more {{what}} through the turns.
payload.template: Steep banking, as at Bristol and Talladega, lets cars carry more {{what}} through the turns.

explanation.correct: Yes. The tilt of the track presses the car into the surface, so steep banking lets cars go faster and creates multi-groove racing.
explanation.incorrect: Banking does not change fuel or weight. The tilt helps the car hold the corner, so it lets cars carry more speed.

payload.prompt: Does dirty air make it easier to pass?

scene.alt: Two cars in traffic, one ahead and one behind, at a fast track.

explanation.correct: Right. Dirty air is the turbulent wake behind a car. It reduces the trailing car's front grip, so it is harder to follow closely and pass.
explanation.incorrect: Dirty air hurts the car behind. It cuts front grip and makes passing harder, which is why clean air up front is valuable.

payload.prompt: Match each term to the 2026 Chase structure.

pairs.definition: The drivers who make the Chase after the 26-race regular season.
Darlington through Homestead; no eliminations, just one long race for points.
Homestead-Miami, race 36, where the most points wins the title.
Seeds 1 to 16 start at 2,100, 2,075, 2,065, 2,060, then drop 5 per seed to 2,000.

distractorDefinitions: The driver with the most wins always makes the Chase.
Eliminations cut the field after every round.

explanation.summary: The 2026 Chase is 16 drivers, ten races, no eliminations and a points reset that gives the regular-season champion a small cushion.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: He scored stage points on lap 100 even though he finished fifth.

options.text: The top ten at each stage end score bonus points, separate from his finish.
Stage points are only for the race winner.
Scoring stage points means he won the stage.

payload.translation: Stage points go to the top ten at each stage end, and they are separate from finish points.

followUps.line: The top ten at each stage end score 10 down to 1, so a mid-field car can collect points along the way.
followUps.why: It shows you understand the two layers of scoring.

followUps.line: Did he gain places late to finish fifth?
followUps.why: It turns the rule into a question about the race.

payload.prompt: Why does a short-track race have more laps than a superspeedway race of similar length?

options.text: Races are set by distance, so shorter laps mean more of them.
Short-track cars are slower, so they need more time.
Every race has the same number of laps.

explanation.correct: Right. Races are set by laps or miles, not time, so a short track needs many more laps to cover the same distance.
explanation.incorrect: Lap counts change by track. Distance is the target, so shorter tracks mean more laps.

lessons.title: Weak spot review
lessons.objective: Review concepts where mastery is below 0.6.

payload.prompt: What does a team's fuel window tell them?

options.text: How many laps a full tank can last, which sets when they must pit.
How fast the car is with a full tank.
Which pit stall to use.

explanation.correct: Right. The fuel window is the range of laps a tank can last. It sets the latest a team can pit, which is why a caution can reshuffle strategy.
explanation.incorrect: It is about range, not speed or the pit stall. The fuel window is how many laps a tank can last.

payload.prompt: The driver radios 'we are tight.' What does the crew chief work on next?

facts.label: Symptom
facts.value: The front end will not turn; the car pushes up the track

facts.label: Next chance
facts.value: A pit stop in a few laps

facts.label: Goal
facts.value: A car that turns without sliding

options.label: Adjust for more front grip or less rear grip.
options.consequence: That is the direction of the fix. Tight means the front is sliding, so the crew wants the front to hold or the rear to let go a little.
considerations: Tire pressure, wedge and the track bar can all help.

options.label: Add extra fuel to settle the car.
options.consequence: Fuel load does not fix a front-end problem, and a heavy car is even harder to turn.
considerations: Fuel is not a balance tool here.
More weight does not help the front.

payload.expertNote: Tight means the front is out of grip. The crew's whole job in that moment is to move grip toward the front.

payload.prompt: At superspeedways, is the Big One a built-in risk of pack racing?

scene.alt: A pack of cars nose-to-tail at a superspeedway.

choices.label: Yes, tight packs make it likely.
No, it is pure bad luck.

explanation.correct: Right. The draft bunches the field nose to tail, so one small mistake can collect many cars. The Big One is a known risk of that style of racing.
explanation.incorrect: It is not random. The draft packs cars together, so one mistake can turn into a multi-car crash.

payload.prompt: An {{strategy}} pits early so fresh tires gain time before rivals stop.
payload.template: An {{strategy}} pits early so fresh tires gain time before rivals stop.

explanation.correct: Yes. The undercut is the classic call: stop first to get fresh tires and gain time before rivals pit.
explanation.incorrect: Undercut means pitting early. The overcut is the opposite: stay out while rivals pit and hope clear track beats their new tires.

payload.prompt: Match each track type to its defining characteristic.

pairs.definition: Under a mile, tight and bumper-to-bumper; Martinsville is the classic.
One to two miles, where aero and handling matter at mid speeds.
Huge, fast ovals like Daytona and Talladega with pack racing and the Big One.
Left and right turns and braking zones, where specialists can shine.

distractorDefinitions: An oval with one groove and no banking anywhere.
A track with no corners at all.

explanation.summary: Track types decide what skills matter: close racing at short tracks, balance at intermediates, pack strategy at superspeedways and braking at road courses.

payload.prompt: A 400-mile race on a 1.5-mile track is about how many laps?

explanation.correct: Right. 400 miles divided by 1.5 miles a lap is about 267 laps, so around 270.
explanation.incorrect: Divide distance by track length: 400 divided by 1.5 is about 267 laps.

payload.prompt: Which of these is a pit road penalty?

options.text: Speeding on pit road.
Changing four tires.
Waving to the crowd.

explanation.correct: Right. Pit road has a posted speed limit that is monitored in zones, and speeding costs track position. Too many men over the wall is another one.
explanation.incorrect: Changing four tires is a normal stop, and waving is fine. Pit road penalties cover speeding, too many men over the wall and box violations.

payload.prompt: On restarts, do drivers choose the inside or outside lane?

scene.alt: A double-file restart with cars in two lanes.

explanation.correct: Right. Under the choose rule, drivers pick inside or outside in running order, so lane choice is a strategy call.
explanation.incorrect: Drivers pick their lane in running order. That makes the choice part of strategy, not an assignment.

lessons.title: Season refresh
lessons.objective: Refresh rules changes and the current season picture.

payload.prompt: What is the biggest format change in 2026 versus 2014-2025?

options.text: No eliminations: the top 16 race ten Chase races and the most points wins.
Wins now guarantee a playoff spot.
All 40 drivers make the Chase.

explanation.correct: Right. 2026 dropped eliminations for a ten-race Chase with no cuts, and the most points after the finale wins.
explanation.incorrect: There is no win-and-in in 2026 and only 16 drivers make the Chase. The big change is that nobody is eliminated along the way.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: He won the race and got 55 points, so he is now in contention.

options.text: A win is worth 55 points now, up from 40, so winning moves the standings a lot.
Wins are worth 200 points.
55 points is a penalty for winning too much.

payload.translation: A win is worth 55 points in 2026, which is a big boost in the championship fight.

followUps.line: It is 55 for first, 35 for second, 34 for third and so on down to 1 for 40th.
followUps.why: It shows you know a win is worth far more than second place.

followUps.line: That is a 20-point gap between first and second, so winning matters a lot.
followUps.why: It connects the rule to why fans care about wins.

payload.prompt: The 2026 championship race (race 36) is held at {{track}} in {{month}}.
payload.template: The 2026 championship race (race 36) is held at {{track}} in {{month}}.

explanation.correct: Yes. Homestead-Miami hosts the finale on November 8, 2026, moving back from Phoenix, which held it from 2020 to 2025.
explanation.incorrect: The 2026 finale returns to Homestead-Miami on November 8. Phoenix hosted it in 2020 to 2025, and Darlington is the first Chase race, not the finale.

payload.prompt: Does horsepower stay the same across all track types in 2026?

scene.alt: Three NASCAR cars at different track types.

choices.label: No, it varies by track type.

explanation.correct: Right. The package changes by track: about 510 hp at superspeedways, 670 at intermediates and 750 at short tracks and road courses, using the tapered spacer.
explanation.incorrect: The tapered spacer changes the power by track type. It is about 510 hp at superspeedways, 670 at intermediates and 750 at short tracks and road courses.

payload.prompt: What did the December 2025 charter settlement do?

options.text: It made charters permanent, with conditions.
It ended charters for 2026.
It cut the Cup field to 36 cars.

explanation.correct: Right. Charters became permanent (evergreen) with conditions, and the six disputed charters went back to 23XI Racing and Front Row Motorsports. The field is still 36 charters plus open spots.
explanation.incorrect: Charters were not ended, and the field is still 40 cars: 36 charters plus four open spots. The settlement made charters permanent, with conditions.

payload.prompt: Why does the car behind go faster when following closely in a draft?

options.text: The lead car cuts the air, so the trailing car meets less resistance.
The lead car's engine pushes the car behind forward.
It is an optical illusion; neither car goes faster.

explanation.correct: Right. The lead car cuts through the air and the trailing car sits in its wake, meeting less drag. Both cars can go faster.
explanation.incorrect: Engines do not push other cars, and the speed is real. Drafting works because the lead car cuts the air for the car behind.

payload.prompt: Caution, 25 laps to go, second on old tires. Stay out or pit?

facts.label: Leader
facts.value: About to pit for fresh tires

facts.label: Tire falloff
facts.value: Low at this track; old tires hold up

options.label: Stay out and take the lead.
options.consequence: You inherit first place. With low tire falloff, old tires hold up, and track position is hard to take back.
considerations: The leader gives up the lead by pitting.

options.label: Pit for four fresh tires.
options.consequence: Fresh tires help on the restart, but you line up behind cars that stayed out, at a track where passing is hard.
considerations: It can work if falloff is high.

payload.expertNote: Stay-out calls depend on tire falloff: when old tires hold up, track position often beats speed.

payload.prompt: Match each flag to what it signals.

pairs.definition: Start or restart of full-speed racing.
Slow down behind the pace car; the order freezes and pit stops happen.
Stop the race completely for a big crash, repairs or weather.
End of race; the first car across wins.

explanation.summary: Five flags control the race flow: green to go, yellow to slow, red to stop, white for the final lap and checkered for the finish.

payload.prompt: Does the regular-season champion start the Chase with a points advantage?

scene.alt: Points reset board showing seed 1 at 2,100 points.

choices.label: Yes, seed 1 gets a head start.
No, all Chase drivers reset to zero.

explanation.correct: Right. Seed 1 starts at 2,100, seed 2 at 2,075, seed 3 at 2,065 and seed 4 at 2,060, then it drops 5 per seed to 2,000 for seed 16.
explanation.incorrect: Drivers do not reset to zero. The regular-season champion starts at 2,100, which is 25 ahead of seed 2 and 100 ahead of seed 16 at 2,000.

payload.prompt: Who holds the Cup record for most wins, with 200?

options.text: Richard Petty
Dale Earnhardt
Jimmie Johnson

explanation.correct: Right. Richard Petty won 200 Cup races, a record that still stands. Earnhardt and Johnson match his seven titles but not his win total.
explanation.incorrect: All three won seven titles, but the 200-win record belongs to Richard Petty.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: The spotter said clear high, so he ran up by the wall.

options.text: Clear high means the high side is open, so moving up was safe.
Clear high means a wreck is ahead.
Clear high tells him to pit this lap.

payload.translation: The spotter told him nothing was on his high side, so he could move up.

followUps.line: Was the spotter watching for a car on his outside?
followUps.why: It shows you know what the spotter is there to do.

followUps.line: Did it help him get a run on the car ahead?
followUps.why: It turns the call into a racing question.

payload.prompt: The {{role}} makes pit calls from the pit box, while the spotter watches traffic from above.
payload.template: The {{role}} makes pit calls from the pit box, while the spotter watches traffic from above.

explanation.correct: Yes. The crew chief is the strategist who decides pit calls and adjustments, and the spotter is the driver's eyes above the track.
explanation.incorrect: The owner funds the team and the jack man lifts the car. Pit calls come from the crew chief.

statement.speaker: fan
statement.text: What did you think of that last restart? You watched it, right?

options.text: Be honest: say you caught parts of it, and ask what she noticed.
Say you watched every lap, even if you did not.
Say restarts are boring and change the subject.

payload.translation: She wants to share what she loved about the restart. Honest curiosity is the warmest response.

followUps.line: I caught some of it. What did you see?
followUps.why: It is honest and gives her the floor.

followUps.line: Did anyone jump it, or was it a clean restart?
followUps.why: It shows you know what to look for on a restart.
